This module needs the provider export. It shows which doctors, nurses and physiotherapists take the orders, and orders by doctor specialty.

Busiest providers

Doctor visits by specialty

The provider export has no specialty yet. In sql/provider_orders_daily.sql, replace NULL::text AS specialty with the column that holds the doctor’s specialty (the query’s comment has a search to find it), then load the export again.

To test whether a specialty moves another service, for example internal medicine and lab tests, open Service links with Doctor visit and Lab tests selected.

Gateway providers: who new patients start with, and do they come back

This needs the gateway export. It shows which provider served each new patient’s first visit, and how many of those patients came back within 30, 90 and 180 days.

  1. In Metabase, create a new SQL question and paste the query (Copy SQL below).
  2. Run it with no date filter, then download the results as CSV.
  3. Open the Data tab and drop the file on the gateway box.

By gateway provider and first service

New patients per month, by gateway provider

Back within 90 days, by cohort month

By first service

How this is worked out
  • The gateway is the provider on a patient’s first-ever real visit (started, finished or reviewed). Services with no provider, like most lab tests, show as No named provider.
  • Back within 30, 90 or 180 days: the patient had a real service in another order within that many days after the first visit. A patient only counts once that many days have passed.
  • vs typical: the provider’s 90-day return minus the median provider’s with the same first service, so one very large or very good provider doesn’t make everyone else look worse. With only one or two providers tested, they’re compared with the others together. Providers with fewer than 20 patients past 90 days aren’t tested. When providers differ from each other more than chance allows, the bar is raised to match.
  • Strong: passes the strict bar, 5% shared across every provider tested. Possible: passes the usual 5% bar for one test only, so with many providers a few turn up by chance. Treat them as leads.
  • A provider can look better because of the patients they get (area, age, reason for the visit), not only how they treat them.
  • The services and dates in the filter bar pick the first service and the cohort month. New patient means (under More filters) picks first visit or account created. Visit status and measure don’t apply here.

Does ad spend move orders?

The ads counted under More filters › Ad spend counts, against orders for the services picked above. To test physio ads against lab tests: pick the Physiotherapy ad group there and choose only Lab tests in Services.

Statistics and method · correlation by lag, the bars used

Change in spend vs change in orders, 0 to 4 weeks later

Passes the barCould be chance

"Strong" passes the 1% bar, which allows for five lags being checked; "possible" passes the usual 5% bar. Both bars are corrected for week-to-week swings (Bartlett). Weekly spend per ad is its monthly spend spread by the account's daily spend, so a single week can be approximate. Correlation shows timing that lines up, not proof that one causes the other.

Do a provider’s patients go on to other services?

For each doctor, nurse and physiotherapist among the selected services: of the patients they saw, the share who had one of the other selected services within 7 and 30 days, against the typical (median) provider of the same service. For example, how many of a doctor’s patients had a lab test afterwards.

30-day follow-on by month

Busy weeks and what followed

When a doctor, nurse or physiotherapist takes an unusually large share of their service in a week, do the other selected services grow faster in the 2 to 4 weeks after? Click a row to see both series.

Weekly share

Busy weekOther week

Service

Full Saturday-to-Friday weeks in the date range. A provider’s share is their week divided by their whole service’s, unassigned included, so a week when everyone is busy doesn’t count as busy. A busy week is at or above the provider’s own 80th percentile, about 1 week in 5. Growth after a week compares the other service’s average over the next 2 (or 4) weeks with its average over that week and the 3 before. Busy weeks are compared with the provider’s other weeks (Welch t-test; the windows overlap, so each group counts as half or a quarter as many weeks). “Strong” passes a 5% bar corrected for every row and both horizons; “possible” passes the usual 5% bar. Each row shows the horizon with the smaller p. Shares within a service add up to 100%, so a colleague’s busy weeks can show the same result reversed. Timing that lines up is not proof that one causes the other.

What inside a service moves the others?

Each doctor specialty and the busiest doctors, nurses and physiotherapists among the selected services, tested against the other selected services: do changes in, say, internal medicine visits line up with changes in lab tests 0 to 4 weeks later? Click a row to see both series.

Driver

Service

"Strong" passes a 5% bar corrected for every pair and lag tested at once, so a chance result rarely passes; "possible" passes the usual 5% bar for a single test, and with many pairs some will pass by chance. Each row shows its best lag. Correlation shows timing that lines up, not proof that one causes the other.

How the selected services move together

Each cell is the correlation of week-to-week changes between the row and the column service, in the same week (1 = always together, 0 = unrelated, negative = opposite). A note shows when the column service moves a few weeks after or before the row service more strongly than in the same week.

Weekly volume side by side

Each service is shown as a share of its own weekly average (100 = a normal week), so services of very different size can be compared on one scale. Hover for the actual numbers.

Does one lead the other?

Correlation of week-over-week changes, with the second service shifted earlier or later. A bar well above zero at +1 means a rise in the first service is usually followed by a rise in the second a week later.

    Same-week links are often shared causes (holidays, ad pushes, salary days) rather than one service driving the other. A link that shows up one or two weeks later is the better sign of one service feeding another. Correlation is not proof of cause.

    One per 100 of the other

    The smaller service per 100 of the larger, by month. A rising line means the smaller service is growing faster, for example more lab tests for every 100 doctor visits.

    Same patients, next service

    Share of patients who had the first service in a month and then the second within 30 days. This is the direct measure of one service leading to another.

    This needs the service follow-on export. Open the Data tab, copy the follow-on SQL, run it in Metabase and drop the CSV there.

    Unique patients

    Each patient counted once per month, by the month of their visit (scheduled time) whatever Dates by is set to. New patients follow the New patient = switch in the filter bar: first-ever visit in that month, or patient record created in that month. Returning = everyone else served that month.

    This section needs one extra Metabase export. The main export counts patients per day, so unique patients can't be worked out from it.

    1. In Metabase, create a new SQL question and paste the query (Copy SQL below).
    2. Run it with no date filter, then download the results as CSV.
    3. Open the Data tab and drop the file on the patients box.

    Unique patients can't be added across months or categories: someone treated in both March and April counts once in each month. For a longer period, compare month by month.

    Meta ads

    Each ad is matched to the service it promotes by its name: first its code (PT, NS, DRV, LT…), then words in the ad name, the ad set name, and finally the campaign name. Recruitment, app-install and awareness campaigns keep their own groups. Corrections go in ad_service_map.csv. Results are counted the way each campaign's objective defines them: WhatsApp conversations for message campaigns, purchases, installs or leads for the others. Cost per order divides spend by orders for the matching services in the same dates, so it is a rough efficiency signal, not attribution.

    Holiday effects

    Orders per day during each holiday compared with the same weekdays in the four weeks before and after. Uses the services and statuses selected above and all available history. Grey years had too little volume to count toward the average.

    Outside factor effects

    Events from the Google Sheet (sudden holidays, salary windows, security and economic events), measured the same way as holidays: orders per day during the event against the same weekdays in the four weeks around it. Campaign launches and events longer than two weeks aren't measured.

    Events log

    Everything in the Saleem Outside Factors Google Sheet except official holidays, which come from the calendar. These are the markers on the trend chart. Add new events to the sheet; ask Claude to check the news and it will add them there too.

    Events you add are saved in this browser only. Use "Copy as CSV" and send them to Claude to make them permanent.

    Competitor milestones

    From the Competitors tab of the Saleem Outside Factors sheet. After is the 4 weeks from the milestone against the 4 weeks before it, for the services picked above, compared with the usual 4-week change over the half year before; negative means orders grew less than usual.

    No competitor milestones yet. Add rows to the Competitors tab of the sheet (date, competitor, milestone, type, services, city, status, source, notes), or ask Claude to research them.
